key: That One Thing, breathless, breathed by its own nature: apart from it was nothing whatsoever.
s: In a hymn asking what was before existent and non-existent and whence creation came, the verse tells what alone there was; Sāyaṇa, on 10.129.2, takes ‘That One Thing’ as Brahman, known throughout the Vedānta, and ‘its own nature’ as māyā, with which it lay undivided.

evidence.words: “तत्” सकलवेदान्तप्रसिद्धं ब्रह्मतत्त्वम् “आनीत्” प्राणितवत्। … स्वस्मिन् धीयते ध्रियत आश्रित्य वर्तत इति स्वधा माया। तया तद्ब्रह्मैकमविभागापन्नमासीत्।
evidence.gloss: ‘That’ is the reality of Brahman, well known throughout the Vedānta; ‘breathed’: it was as though breathing. … Svadhā (‘its own nature’) is what is placed and held in oneself, what exists resting on it: māyā. With it that Brahman was one, having come to be undivided.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref and at match). The plain sense places the verse in the creation hymn, which describes the state when neither existent nor non-existent was and asks whence creation came: faithful. In the Sanskrit packet at 10.129.2 Sāyaṇa glosses tat as the reality of Brahman well known in all the Vedānta and svadhā as māyā, with which that Brahman was one, undivided (avibhāgāpannam); Wilson’s note (printed with 10.129.1 to 3) confirms he takes svadhā as Māyā. The reading carries his words without drift; revision 402226 dated 2024 by the Wikisource API; gate ok.
